new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Information on the role of stress is insufficient; however, there are grounds to believe that it had no meaning-distinguishing (contrastive) function.
new_statements.citation: Nosnitsyn, D.A. 2013. Gafat jazyk. In M.S. Bulakh, L.E. Kogan, O.I. Romanova (eds.), Jazyki mira: Semitskie jazyki. Efiosemitskie jazyki, 546-576. Moskva: Academia.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (622 pp., text layer present; extracted text). Printed p. 549 = PDF p. 549, header 'Д.А. Носницын. Гафат язык', carries exactly: '2.1.2. Сведений о роли ударения недостаточно, однако есть основания полагать, что оно не имело смыслоразличительной функции.' -- verbatim as reported (also line 26846 of dump and). Read the surrounding phonology (2.1.1 consonant/vowel inventory, gemination contrastive; 2.1.3 alternations; 2.1.4 syllable structure) and grepped the whole chapter pp. 546-576 for ударен/акцент/тон: the 2.1.2 sentence is the only mention of stress; the only other prosodic remark is that yes/no questions are marked by rising intonation or the particle wäy. So the source…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in Gafat is reported as non-contrastive (no lexical/grammatical distinctions carried by stress); the source explicitly says the data are insufficient and gives no rule for the position of stress. Consistent with Hetzron 1997:539 (stress 'not relevant' in Outer South Ethiopic generally except Peripheral Western Gurage), Leslau 1966 sec. 1.8 ('not easily perceptible in the word' in most Ethiopic languages) and Hyman 1977's listing of Gafat under 'no stress-accent'.
new_statements.domain_note: No domain specified; statement concerns the phonological (non-)function of stress only. The sketch is compiled from Leslau's 1947 fieldwork with the last four speakers (published 1956) and the 18th-c. written documents (Leslau 1945); the language is extinct, so no modern first-hand data exist.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Gafat as a single variety (Nosnitsyn 2.7.0: no dialect information). Modern statements rest on Leslau's 1947 recordings of four elderly rememberers in Wämbärma district, Gojjam, whose Gafat was already partly Amharicized (Voigt 2005); the 1945 'Gafat Documents' describe an 18th-century written text and cannot bear on stress.
